title: The country parson
hookLine: George Herbert on the pastor who visits, teaches and prays through the ordinary

lines: OUT THE DOOR ON A WEEKDAY.
cards: A small book with a long title: A Priest to the Temple, or, The Country Parson.
Its author, George Herbert, first met back on day eight hundred eighty-three, was a poet and a priest of the Church of England who served a small country parish.

In short chapters he sets down what a good pastor does: how he lives, preaches, comforts, and runs his house. One chapter follows him out the door on an ordinary weekday afternoon, walking from house to house.
Not on Sunday, when everyone is ready for him. On a plain weekday, when nobody is. Today: the country parson.

teach.h: FIND THEM AS THEY REALLY ARE.
teach.b: Herbert's reason for the weekday visit is simple, and a little sly. On Sunday, people come to church dressed up and on their best behavior.
On a weekday afternoon the parson finds them as they really are, in the middle of their work and their troubles, and that's where he can actually help.

So he goes from house to house: comforting the sick, praising the hard-working, admonishing the idle, giving to those in need, and, where it's welcome, praying with them right there among the pots and tools.
The Bible behind this is plain.

teach.h: I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.
teach.b: In Jesus's picture of the last judgment, the king says, "I was sick, and ye visited me."

The letter of James puts it more bluntly: "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction." Herbert's poems say it from the inside.

teach.h: WHO SWEEPS A ROOM, AS FOR THY LAWS.
teach.b: In one called The Elixir, he asks God to teach him to see God in all things, then lands here: "Who sweeps a room, as for thy laws, / Makes that and th' action fine." Sweeping. Not a vision, not a cathedral.
A broom. That's Herbert's Anglican way: holiness in the ordinary parish, week and room. Not every Christian has a parson.
Some have a pastor, a priest, an elder, a small-group leader, or a neighbor who simply shows up.
But the picture travels: someone who knows the street, knocks on the door, and sits down at the kitchen table in the middle of the mess.

how: In parish life, Anglican clergy and lay visitors call on the sick, the housebound and the grieving at home, and some clergy still read Herbert's The Country Parson as a picture of a pastor's work.

games.why: Herbert sends the parson out on weekday afternoons. on Sunday people are on their best behavior; on a weekday he finds them as they are, and can help.

practice: Let a face come to mind: someone sick, someone alone, someone you haven't sat with in a while.

See yourself knocking, being let in, sitting down in the middle of their day, and ask what you could bring: soup, a card, an hour, or a call if a visit isn't possible. If you pray, hold that person before God now, by name.

wordCard.voice: The country parson. George Herbert's picture of a pastor who lives among his people, visits them on ordinary days, and finds God in ordinary work.

orig.note: Greek: to look in on, to visit and care for — the verb behind "visit" in James 1:27 and Matthew 25:36.

carryVoice: Your line: the ordinary parish. The week ran from a Celtic circle to a knock at the door. See you tomorrow.
